learn.title: Flow Batteries for Grid Storage
learn.intro: Flow batteries store energy in liquid electrolytes, offering scalable, long-duration storage for renewable grids. Ideal for balancing solar/wind intermittency, they enable cleaner energy transitions without fossil fuel backups.
learn.c1_text: Flow batteries use liquid electrolytes stored in tanks. Energy is stored chemically and released via redox reactions. Unlike lithium-ion, they scale easily—1 MW power/10 MWh storage possible, perfect for grid stability.
learn.c2_text: Vanadium redox batteries use same element in both electrolytes, avoiding cross-contamination. Iron-flow systems are cheaper but less efficient (70-80% vs. 75-85%). Both offer 20,000+ cycles, far outlasting lithium-ion.
learn.c3_text: India’s 500 MW target by 2030 includes pilot projects like NTPC’s 20 MWh system. With ₹4/kWh subsidies, iron-flow adoption could cut storage costs by 40%, supporting 500 GW renewable goals.
learn.stat1: India: 500 MW flow battery target by 2030

learn.title: Wind Turbine Electricity Generation
learn.intro: Wind turbines convert kinetic energy into electricity via spinning blades and generators. They power 6% of global electricity, reducing reliance on coal and gas.
learn.c1_text: Blades capture wind energy through lift principles. At 12 m/s wind speed, a 2 MW turbine generates ~4.3 MW (capacity factor 35%). Longer blades (e.g., 80m) increase output by 20% per meter.
learn.c2_text: Synchronous generators convert mechanical rotation to AC electricity. Gearboxes amplify blade rotation (15-20 RPM) to 1,000-1,800 RPM for efficient power conversion.
learn.c3_text: India has 44 GW wind capacity (2024), with 60% from onshore. Tamil Nadu leads with 10 GW, supported by policies like the National Wind Energy Mission.
learn.stat2: 2 MW turbine output: ~4.3 MW at 12 m/s

learn.title: Virtual Power Plants (VPPs)
learn.intro: VPPs aggregate distributed energy sources (solar, batteries) using AI to optimize grid supply. They stabilize grids and reduce peak demand by 25-30% in pilot programs.
learn.c1_text: AI algorithms predict and balance supply-demand in real-time. For example, 100,000 smart meters in a VPP can adjust 500 MW collectively, mimicking a traditional power plant.
learn.c2_text: VPPs manage solar, wind, EVs, and storage. In California, a 200 MW VPP reduced grid strain during heatwaves by dispatching 10,000 home batteries.
learn.c3_text: India’s 50 GW rooftop solar potential could integrate into VPPs. The 2023 National Electricity Policy proposes AI-driven VPPs to manage variability.

learn.title: Hydrogen Fuel Cells in Vehicles
learn.intro: Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen, emitting only water. They power vehicles with zero emissions, ideal for heavy transport.
learn.c1_text: Protons from hydrogen combine with oxygen in a catalyst, generating 0.7 V per cell. A 60 kW fuel cell stack powers a sedan, achieving 60% efficiency vs. 20% for internal combustion engines.
learn.c2_text: Fuel cells power electric motors via inverters. Toyota Mirai’s 1.6 kW stack provides 650 km range, refueled in 5 minutes—comparable to gasoline cars.
learn.c3_text: India’s 2023 National Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MTPA green hydrogen by 2030. Pilot projects like NELCO’s 10 MW plant aim to cut fuel cell costs by 30%.

learn.title: Offshore Wind Farms
learn.intro: Offshore wind farms harness stronger coastal winds, generating 30-40% more power than onshore. They require specialized turbines and grid connection systems.
learn.c1_text: Turbines are larger (15 MW units) with corrosion-resistant materials. The 150-meter Haliade-X rotor captures 20% more energy than onshore counterparts.
learn.c2_text: Floating platforms anchor turbines in deep water. Installation costs are 25% higher than onshore, but lifetime output offsets this via 40+ year lifespans.
learn.c3_text: India’s 30 GW offshore target includes the 1 GW Mumbai Offshore Wind Project. The 2022 National Offshore Wind Policy streamlines permits and R&D funding.

learn.title: Small Wind Turbines
learn.intro: Small turbines (<100 kW) generate local power for homes or communities. They reduce grid dependence and are ideal for remote areas with consistent wind.
learn.c1_text: A 5 kW turbine produces ~10,000 kWh/year at 6 m/s wind. Paired with batteries, it can meet 30-50% of a home’s needs, cutting electricity bills by ₹15,000 annually.
learn.c2_text: Turbines require sustained winds >4 m/s. India’s western ghats and coastal areas (e.g., Maharashtra) have 200+ sites with >5 m/s wind, per CEA data.
learn.c3_text: Kerala’s 200 kW turbine powers 50 homes in a village. The 2022 MNRE policy offers ₹1.5 lakh subsidies, accelerating rural adoption.
